# Isaiah 46 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter divides naturally into four sections (Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges, via biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/46.htm):

1. **vv. 1–4** — A contrast between the Babylonian gods and the God of Israel: the idols are borne away in humiliating flight; Jehovah *bears* His people.
2. **vv. 5–7** — A sarcastic exposé of idolatry (the fourth such passage in Isaiah, following 40:18–20; 41:6–7; 44:9–20).
3. **vv. 8–11** — A renewed appeal to the argument from prophecy: God declares the end from the beginning and summons Cyrus.
4. **vv. 12–13** — The announcement of speedy deliverance for Zion.

G. Campbell Morgan (via preceptaustin.org) captures the chapter's central contrast succinctly: "An idol is a thing which a man makes, and has to carry. The true God makes the man, and carries him."

---

## v. 1 — *"Bel crouches; Nebo cowers. Their idols weigh down beasts and cattle. The images you carry are burdensome, a load to the weary animal."*

- **Bel and Nebo identified.** Bel (from Babylonian *Bilu* or *Belu*, meaning "lord") was the title for Marduk (Merodach), the chief god of Babylon, worshipped at the great temple Etemenanki. Nebo (Nabu) was the god of learning and prophecy — a kind of Assyrian Hermes — and the patron deity of Borsippa. Both names appear in Babylonian royal names: Belshazzar, Nebuchadnezzar, Nabonassar, Nabopolassar. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm; Pulpit Commentary, biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/46.htm; Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **The imagery of "crouching" and "cowering."** The prophet pictures the fall of Babylon's gods in material terms — their images being torn from shrines and loaded onto pack animals as plunder. Jarchi (cited by Gill) notes the verbs can carry a crude, sarcastic sense (like men doubled over in colic). Aben Ezra acknowledged the crude sense but considered it unfit to write. Whatever the exact nuance, the mockery is deliberate: these mighty gods are reduced to luggage. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **"Your carriages" / "the things you carried."** The Hebrew refers to the images that were once carried in joyful festival procession (as in the Babylonian New Year's festival in April, when images of Marduk and Nabu were paraded). Now they are packed as dead weight onto weary beasts. Ellicott notes that Herodotus (1:183) records Xerxes eventually carrying off the golden image of Bel — the grandson fulfilling what Cyrus left undone. (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm; Layman's Bible Commentary, studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/isaiah-46.html)

- **David Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** "God gets personal, 'naming names' when it comes to idols; and now these false gods are brought low." The names Bel and Nebo live on in Belshazzar and Nebuchadnezzar — showing how deeply embedded these gods were in Babylonian identity. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

- **Kretzmann (Lutheran – LCMS):** Bel is described as "the highest deity of Babylon" who "boweth down, is fallen." The statues, once carried by priests in solemn procession, are now "loaded upon pack-animals, which dragged along, weary with the heavy load." This prepares the way for a "sharp reproof of Israel for its idolatrous leanings." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-46.html)

---

## v. 2 — *"The gods cower; they crouch together, unable to relieve the burden; but they themselves go into captivity."*

- **"They could not deliver the burden."** Ellicott notes a crucial distinction: the deities are momentarily distinguished from their images. They are powerless even to rescue their own statues. "So far as they have a soul or being at all, that very being is carried away captive." (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **"Their souls" — a derisive phrase.** Gill observes that the Hebrew can be read "their souls" (*animae eorum*, Vulgate), spoken in mockery of inanimate idols that have no soul at all. The phrase also echoes the idea that what was dearest to the Babylonians — their gods — is now taken. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The bottom line: "They could not deliver the burden, but have themselves gone into captivity." Even the idols are loaded onto the moving trucks. This is total humiliation. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

- **Constable (Evangelical):** Notes an irony: the gods that were supposed to carry the nation end up creating burdens for the people. "Rather than lifting burdens, these idols created them for their worshippers." The prophet foresees the idols being carried into captivity by Cyrus, powerless to help. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt)

---

## v. 3 — *"Listen to Me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been sustained from the womb, carried along since birth."*

- **The great reversal.** Ellicott calls the word choice "singularly emphatic." The false gods are *borne away* as a burden; the true God *bears* His people. "He is able to bear that burden. Every 'I' is emphasised in the Hebrew." (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **"From the belly … from the womb."** The language evokes tender parental care. Gill notes the Lord took pity on Israel from its infancy as a nation — bearing them as a father bears a son through the wilderness (Numbers 11:12; Deuteronomy 1:31). Applied spiritually, the language also describes God's care for the regenerate person from the moment of new birth. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **"The remnant."** The address is to faithful Israel — those who remain after judgment. Gill identifies these spiritually as "those who are Israelites indeed … the remnant according to the election of grace." (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan):** "The prophet very ingeniously, and with great force, contrasts the power of God, and his tender goodness … with the inability of the false gods. He like an indulgent father had carried his people in his arms." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt)

- **Guzik:** The irony Isaiah exposes is stark — false gods must be carried; the true God carries His people "from before their birth." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

---

## v. 4 — *"Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray. I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you."*

- **"Even to your old age I am He."** Ellicott notes the profound tenderness: "The care of a mother ceases, in the natural course of things, before a man grows old, but the fatherly, we might almost say the mother-like, maternal care of Jehovah for His chosen ones endures even to the end of life." (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Spurgeon (Baptist) — a full sermon on this verse (No. 81, "The God of the Aged").** Spurgeon holds the doctrine of the text to be "the constancy of God's love, its perpetuity, and its unchangeable nature." God is not simply the God of young saints or middle-aged saints, but "the God of the saints in all their ages from the cradle to the tomb." He notes that Lowth translates it, "Even to old age I am the same." The doctrine is twofold: God Himself is the same whatever our age, and His dealings toward us — "His carryings and His deliverings" — are alike unchanged. (spurgeon.org/sermons/the-god-of-the-aged; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/isaiah-46.html)

- **Spurgeon devotional (via Precept Austin):** "When the road is smooth, I have to walk, but when it is very rough, I am carried … Any sensible child of God will still say, 'Carry me, Father! Carry me still!' The Father's answer is, 'I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry … you.'" (preceptaustin.org/isaiah_devotionals_4)

- **"I have made, and I will bear."** Gill: God made these persons not merely as creatures but as *new creatures* — "they are formed for myself; they are my sons and daughters." Therefore He will bear them from regeneration to glory. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Whedon (Methodist):** The prophet shows the nation differently cared for by Jehovah, who attended "its birth at the exodus, its infancy in the desert, its manhood under David and Solomon, its old age under the later prophets, when the first covenant was ready to decay." Idols do no such thing. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt)

- **Guzik:** Compares this to Jesus' words in Luke 12:6–7 about the sparrows and the hairs of the head. "It's a worthy question: do you have to carry your gods, or does your God carry you?" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

- **Kretzmann (Lutheran):** God's promise extends "to the most advanced age of their history, to the very end of their national existence." The fact that He has sustained them in the past is the guarantee for the future. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-46.html)

---

## v. 5 — *"To whom will you liken Me or count Me equal? To whom will you compare Me, that we should be alike?"*

- **Resumption of the polemic against idolatry.** Ellicott notes that this renews the argument in nearly its old form (Isaiah 40:18–25; 44:9–17). The fate of Bel and Nebo is now used as evidence: after witnessing their humiliation, how could anyone think of likening Jehovah to them? The sin of the golden calves at Bethel and Dan is in view. (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Kretzmann:** "The heaping of expressions again stresses the uniqueness of the true God … How is it possible for Israel even to think of placing the true God on a level with the heathen idols after the manifestations of His power and mercy which they have witnessed?" (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-46.html)

- **Gill:** No creature in heaven or earth can be likened to the One who has shown such tender care for His people "from the beginning of their state to the close of it." The question is rhetorical — the answer is obvious: nothing and no one. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

---

## v. 6 — *"They pour out their bags of gold and weigh out silver on scales; they hire a goldsmith to fashion it into a god, so they can bow down and worship."*

- **"They lavish gold out of the bag."** Gill distinguishes two types of idolaters: the lavish, who pour out gold profusely regardless of cost, and the stingy, who carefully weigh out silver with a scale to avoid being cheated. Both are equally foolish — the rich man's golden idol and the poor man's silver one are identically helpless. Gill also notes that money was not yet coined but weighed. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Constable:** This is Isaiah's fourth and final exposé of the folly of idol worship (cf. 40:19–20; 41:6–7; 44:9–20). "How foolish it is to spend a lot of money and effort to make something that cannot care for itself much less its worshipper." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt)

- **Guzik:** "Much money and attention are given to the production and care of our idols." The irony is unmistakable: people spend fortunes on what cannot help them. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

---

## v. 7 — *"They lift it to their shoulder and carry it along; they set it in its place, and there it stands, not budging from that spot. They cry out to it, but it does not answer; it saves no one from his troubles."*

- **A sarcastic description of utter helplessness.** Gill notes the sequence: the idol must be lifted (it cannot lift itself), carried (it cannot walk), set in its place (it cannot stand on its own), and once there it cannot move. It has to be nailed down. Then the worshipper cries out — but gets nothing. Gill references 1 Kings 18:26 (the prophets of Baal) and Psalm 115:5. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **The progressive absurdity.** Guzik highlights each step: bear it, carry it, set it, it stands, it shall not move, it cannot answer, it cannot save. Each clause drives the mockery deeper. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

- **Kretzmann:** The idol is "a dead thing unable to move." When the worshipper cries out, the idol can neither answer nor save him "out of his trouble." The helplessness of idols is set before the people yet again. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-46.html)

---

## v. 8 — *"Remember this and be brave; take it to heart, you transgressors!"*

- **"Show yourselves men" / "be brave."** The Hebrew verb (*hith'oshashu*) can be read several ways. Ellicott says the phrase is couched in "the language of irony" — idol-worshippers should at least have the courage of their convictions. A conjectural emendation yields the opposite sense: "Be ye deeply ashamed." (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Gill catalogs the range of translations:** The Targum and Jarchi read "be ye strong" (fortify yourselves against idolatry). Rabenu Hal and Joseph Kimchi read "burn ye" or "be ye inflamed" — i.e., blush and be ashamed. The Vulgate has "be ye confounded." Vitringa: "be fired with zeal for God and His glory, and with indignation against such gross idolatry." (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **"Transgressors."** The address is to those who have forgotten the covenant — likely Israelites who had been drawn into Babylonian idolatry. Whedon says: "Learn the lesson of the impotence of idol gods to give aid; learn to stand firm, and resist staunchly the whole idol system." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Guzik:** "We can gain the courage of men when we remember the things God tells us to remember. How much defeat we suffer in the Christian life through simply forgetting." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

---

## v. 9 — *"Remember what happened long ago, for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me."*

- **"I am God" — two different Hebrew words.** Ellicott notes: the first predicate is *El* (the Mighty and Strong One), the second is *Elohim* (the one true object of worship). The verse that follows asserts what modern theology calls the omniscience and omnipotence of God. (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **"Remember the former things of old."** Gill lists examples: the creation of the heavens and earth, the destruction of the old world, the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, the Exodus from Egypt — all proofs of the true deity of the God of Israel over against the idols. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Kretzmann:** The reference is to "the miracles of God which happened in the earliest history of Israel" (see 43:18). The foretelling of future events is "one of the chief proofs of His divinity." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-46.html)

- **Guzik:** "God knows the end of every matter, of every course of circumstances, just as clearly as anyone else can see the beginning of it." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

---

## v. 10 — *"I declare the end from the beginning, and ancient times from what is still to come. I say, 'My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish.'"*

- **God's omniscience and sovereignty.** Ellicott: This asserts what modern language would call God's omniscience (declaring the end from the beginning) and omnipotence (accomplishing all His pleasure). (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **"My counsel shall stand."** Gill: The purposes and decrees of God "are within Himself, wisely formed by Him, eternal and not frustrable." Whether regarding providence (the world in general, particular persons) or grace (election, covenant, redemption, effectual calling, glorification), all "stand firm and sure, and shall have their full accomplishment." (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Guzik:** "God isn't just watching the entire parade of history, He is directing the parade." The essential point is that God's people must remember that He knows the end from the beginning and controls all things. "When we remember this, we will show yourselves men." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

- **Spurgeon (Precept Austin devotional on v.10):** "World events are not tangled, confused, or perplexing to God … Jehovah's power is apparent, from the least to the greatest … God is the dictator of destinies. He appoints both the ideas and the end. He is the King of kings, ruling rulers and guiding counselors." (preceptaustin.org/isaiah_devotionals_4)

---

## v. 11 — *"I summon a bird of prey from the east, a man for My purpose from a far-off land. Truly I have spoken, and truly I will bring it to pass. I have planned it, and I will surely do it."*

- **Cyrus as the "bird of prey" / "ravenous bird."** All the commentaries agree this is Cyrus. Ellicott notes that the image derives special force from the fact that "the standard borne by Cyrus and his successors was a golden eagle" (Xenophon, *Cyropaedia* vii.1.4; *Anabasis* i.10.12). Persia is "the sun-rising" (east); "the far country" probably represents Media. (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **"Swift bird" rather than "ravenous."** Gill notes that the Hebrew word denotes more swiftness than rapaciousness — fitting Cyrus, who was renowned for speed in his military campaigns. Xenophon repeatedly commends Cyrus's emphasis on "celerity and dispatch." The Targum renders it "a swift bird." Aben Ezra says Cyrus is so called "as if he flew to do the will of God." (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Guzik:** "God's people need to remember that God always has a deliverer for His people, even if He has to find one among pagan kings." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

- **Constable:** "God had throughout history predicted how history would unfold … Most recently He had predicted Cyrus, who would descend on Babylon like an eagle on a rabbit. His audience could count on this prediction coming to pass." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt)

- **Kretzmann:** "The unquestioned authority of the Lord is combined with his ability to carry out his plans, to realize His projects, something in which He differed most radically from the dead idols." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-46.html)

---

## v. 12 — *"Listen to Me, you stubborn people, far removed from righteousness:"*

- **"Stout-hearted" / "stubborn."** Ellicott notes the word (like similar terms in Ezekiel 2:4; 3:7) "implies at once obduracy and ignorance." Such people are "self-excluded at once from the 'righteousness' and the 'salvation' of Jehovah, which ultimately imply, and coincide with each other." Yet their unfaithfulness does not hinder God's faithfulness. (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Who is addressed?** Constable notes a debate: some interpret the "stubborn-hearted" as the Babylonians, but most (including Motyer) take it as Israelites who found it hard to believe God would deliver them — "far short of fulfilling the righteous act of believing God." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt)

- **Kretzmann:** These are "those who were willingly hardening their hearts against the influence of the Lord, that are far from righteousness, who have excluded themselves from the salvation promised in the Lord's covenant." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-46.html)

- **Guzik:** "When we are stubborn-hearted we need to listen to the LORD and remember He never delays and is never late." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

---

## v. 13 — *"I am bringing My righteousness near; it is not far away, and My salvation will not be delayed. I will grant salvation to Zion and adorn Israel with My splendor."*

- **Righteousness and salvation conjoined.** Ellicott notes that these two ultimately "imply, and coincide with each other." God brings near His salvation to all who are ready to receive it (compare Isaiah 56:1). (Ellicott, biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Gill:** The deliverance by Cyrus is in view but also, ultimately, the salvation by Christ. "Righteousness" here means "the righteousness of God … which justifies sinners." This righteousness and salvation are brought near in the Gospel, set before stubborn-hearted Jews who are "far from righteousness" — yet the offer stands. (Gill, biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/46.htm)

- **Kretzmann (Lutheran):** The promise of salvation in Zion and glory in Israel ultimately points to "the happy condition of the Messianic period." The chapter closes with the sure promise that "salvation in Zion, glory and honor in Israel, in the midst of his Church" shall be realized. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-46.html)

- **Guzik:** "God's people need to remember that God's timing is always precise and wise … God always has His deliverer, and always knows exactly when to bring His deliverance." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-46/)

- **Whedon (Methodist):** The earlier reference to Cyrus carries forward into the Messianic blessings which follow. The deliverance from Babylon is a type of the greater deliverance to come. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt)

- **Constable:** God would be faithful to His covenant promises and bring salvation to Zion. He cross-references Romans 3:21–25; 5:8; 1 Corinthians 1:30 — noting that God "would soon bring the righteousness that His people lacked." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-46.html, via search excerpt)

---

## Points of Tradition-Specific Emphasis

### Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill)
The strongest emphasis falls on **v. 4** as a promise of God's persevering grace. Spurgeon preached an entire sermon ("The God of the Aged," No. 81) on the constancy of God's love — that He is the God of His saints "in all their ages from the cradle to the tomb." Gill emphasizes the spiritual application to the regenerate, who are "carried" from new birth to glory. Both see the chapter as speaking to the perseverance of the saints — God will not abandon His own.

### Methodist / Wesleyan (Clarke, Whedon)
Clarke stresses the "tender goodness" of God's fatherly care, contrasted with the helplessness of idols. Whedon traces God's carrying of Israel through national history — birth at the Exodus, infancy in the desert, manhood under David and Solomon, old age under the later prophets. The emphasis is on God's faithfulness across the whole sweep of salvation history, with the deliverance from Babylon seen as a type of Messianic deliverance.

### Lutheran (Kretzmann – LCMS)
The chapter is read with an eye to the Messianic fulfillment. The deliverance from Babylon is historical, but the ultimate reference of v.13 is to "the happy condition of the Messianic period" — salvation placed in Zion for "Israel My glory" points to the Church and the coming of Christ. The law–gospel dynamic is implicit: the "stout-hearted" who are far from righteousness (law) are nevertheless promised a righteousness brought near (gospel).

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Guzik – Enduring Word)
The chapter is read as a contrast between dead idols and the living God who carries His people. The application is strongly pastoral and personal: "Do you have to carry your gods, or does your God carry you?" Emphasis falls on *remembering* — that "much Christian defeat comes from forgetting rather than from God's failure." The tone is devotional and aimed at encouragement in present trials.

### Anglican (Ellicott)
Ellicott brings philological precision (e.g., *El* vs. *Elohim* in v.9, the emphatic "I" in the Hebrew of vv.3–4) and historical awareness (Cyrus's golden eagle standard from Xenophon, the Cyrus Cylinder inscription). The tone is scholarly yet accessible, with attention to the literary structure and the ironic contrast between the gods who are carried and the God who carries.

## What Could Not Be Found

- **Reformed (Ligonier, Monergism, The Gospel Coalition):** Searches were not completed due to tool limits. Reformed commentators (such as E.J. Young or Alec Motyer — referenced by Constable) would likely emphasize God's sovereign decree in v.10 and unconditional election in the address to "the remnant" in v.3.
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings (New Advent, Catholic.com, OCA.org):** Searches were not completed. Catholic commentary would likely note the liturgical use of this chapter and may connect the idol polemic to the Church's rejection of idolatry; Orthodox reading might emphasize the *theosis* dimension of v.13 ("adorn Israel with My splendor").
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey, NET Bible notes):** Searches were not completed. The NET Bible notes would likely discuss text-critical issues, particularly the Cyrus Cylinder's portrayal of Cyrus as a worshipper of Bel and Nebo (noted by Ellicott as a potential historical tension with the prophecy).
- **Debated modern teachings (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** No specific material surfaced from the allowed sites. A prosperity reading might seize on v.4 ("I will sustain you and deliver you") as a promise of material provision; a hyper-grace reading might emphasize v.13's "righteousness near" as entirely apart from human effort. These are inferences from known tendencies, not from the sites consulted.
